Acacia.note: Flat-topped thorn trees, browsed to their characteristic silhouette by giraffe.

Adansonia.note: The baobab, storing water in a massively swollen trunk -- the signature tree of seasonally arid Africa.

Aglaophyton.note: From the Rhynie chert, and the earliest clear evidence of arbuscular mycorrhizal symbiosis - land plants have always been partly fungal.

Araucaria.note: Still living - monkey puzzle and Norfolk Island pine are the same genus that dominated Jurassic forests.

Araucariaceae.note: Monkey-puzzle and kauri relatives: worldwide in the Mesozoic, southern-hemisphere survivors today.

Araucarioxylon.note: The conifer whose logs make the Petrified Forest, transported and buried in seasonal river systems.

Archaefructus.note: An aquatic Jehol plant that is among the earliest fossils confidently identified as a flowering plant.

Archaeocalamites.note: An early horsetail of the Mississippian wetlands, ancestral to the giant Calamites that would build the coal swamps.

Archaeopteris.note: The first plant with a woody trunk and a true leafy canopy -- effectively the first modern-looking tree.
Archaeopteris.hb: the first true forest tree: real wood, roots to ~1 m, a spreading crown

Arecaceae (palms).note: Palms. In the Eocene hothouse they grew at fifty degrees north beside crocodiles; their limit has been a frost line ever since.

Asteroxylon.note: An early lycophyte with leaf-like enations along a branching stem, and rooting structures that are not yet true roots.

Azolla.note: A floating freshwater fern whose Arctic Ocean blooms buried enough carbon to help end the Eocene hothouse.

Banksia.note: Banksias of the kwongan heath, one of the world's richest floras on the poorest soil.

Baragwanathia.note: A lycophyte with real leaves, appearing surprisingly early in Australia and complicating every tidy story about plant evolution.
Baragwanathia.hb: creeping and upright shoots with true microphylls

Bennettitales.note: Cycad-like plants with tight, flower-like cones that were probably insect pollinated. An independent Mesozoic run at the flower that left no descendants.

Betula.note: Birch: a pioneer tree that follows retreating ice, and one of the first to colonise ground left bare by a glacier.

Botrychiopsis.note: A cold-climate seed plant of the floras that recolonised bare ground as the Karoo ice sheets melted.

Bouteloua gracilis.note: Blue grama, the shortgrass prairie's dominant sod-former.

Bromeliaceae.note: Epiphytic bromeliads holding tank-pools in the canopy, each its own small ecosystem.

C4 grasses.note: Grasses using the C4 photosynthetic pathway, which is efficient in warm, dry, low-CO2 air. They build tropical savanna from about 8 Ma.

Calamites.note: Tree-sized horsetails forming dense stands along channel margins.
Calamites.hb: clonal thickets on levees and channel margins

Calamophyton.note: A cladoxylopsid tree from the oldest forest floors known. It shed whole branches rather than leaves, and its roots began cracking rock into soil and drawing CO2 out of the air.

Callipteris (Autunia).note: The seed fern that marks the Permian red beds across Euramerica: the flora of a continent that had lost its swamps.

Calluna vulgaris.note: Heather: the low evergreen shrub that makes the moorland of Atlantic Europe, on poor, acid, often burnt ground.

Cathaysiodendron.note: A lycopsid tree of the Cathaysian coal forests of South China -- the rainforests that kept growing after the Euramerican ones collapsed.

Ceiba pentandra.note: The kapok, an emergent tree standing above the canopy with buttress roots metres tall.

Cheirolepidiaceae.note: A drought-tolerant conifer family whose Classopollis pollen swamps Jurassic and Cretaceous lowland sediments: the canopy many sauropods fed in.

Cooksonia.note: A few centimetres of leafless forking stem with a spore capsule on top: the first vascular plant, and the ancestor of every forest.
Cooksonia.hb: tiny dichotomising axes in damp lowlands

Cordaites.note: Strap-leaved coniferophytes up to thirty metres tall on the drier ground beyond the mires: the first vegetation that would read as forest rather than swamp.
Cordaites.hb: tree with strap-shaped leaves; coastal and upland

Cyperus papyrus.note: Papyrus sedge, forming floating swamps along African rivers and lake margins.

Deschampsia antarctica.note: Antarctic hairgrass, one of just two flowering plants on the continent.

Dicroidium.note: The forked-leaf seed fern that defines Gondwanan Triassic forest and marks the end of the coal gap.

Dipterocarpaceae.note: Dipterocarps, which dominate South-East Asian rainforest to a degree no family manages anywhere else, and mast-fruit across whole regions at once.

Elkinsia.note: One of the earliest seed plants; the seed is what eventually lets vegetation leave the water's edge.

Eospermatopteris.note: The tree of the Gilboa 'forest' in New York - the oldest known forest, of fern-like Wattieza trees.

Eucalyptus.note: Gum trees. Eucalypts and charcoal rise together through the Miocene record: fire and aridity remaking a rainforest continent. Their oldest fossils, oddly, are from Patagonia.

Fagus.note: Beech, a dominant temperate deciduous tree casting shade too deep for most competitors.

Gangamopteris.note: As glossopteris but with non-midribbed leaves
Gangamopteris.hb: as Glossopteris but with non-midribbed leaves

Gigantopteris.note: A Cathaysian seed plant with broad net-veined leaves that look startlingly like an angiosperm's, 150 million years early.
Gigantopteris.hb: climbing or scrambling, with large net-veined leaves

Ginkgo.note: One species survives; the genus was near-global in the Jurassic and Cretaceous.

Ginkgoales.note: The ginkgo lineage at its widest, in mid-latitude forests on nearly every continent. One species, Ginkgo biloba, is still alive.

Glossopteris.note: A tongue-leaved seed fern blanketing Gondwana, whose distribution across five now-separate continents was early evidence for continental drift.
Glossopteris.hb: woody tree in very wet soils, like a modern bald cypress; conical, widely spaced crowns to exploit low-angle polar light

Heliamphora.note: Sun-pitcher plants trapping insects on nutrient-starved sandstone summits.

Kobresia.note: Tough, mat-forming sedges whose turf makes the vast alpine meadows of high Asia and the Arctic.

Larix.note: Larch -- the deciduous conifer, dropping its needles to survive the extreme continental winters of interior Siberia.

Larix decidua.note: The European larch, a deciduous conifer at the timberline.

Larix gmelinii.note: Dahurian larch, the only tree that forms forest on continuous permafrost.

Lepidodendrales.note: Scale trees beginning their takeover of coastal mires -- the coal machine is warming up.

Lepidodendron.note: A thirty-metre lycopsid that grew fast, reproduced once and toppled -- the principal ingredient of coal.
Lepidodendron.hb: unbranched pole with a crown, DETERMINATE growth - grew, reproduced once, died

Lobatannularia.note: A horsetail relative with whorls of broad leaves, characteristic of the Cathaysian flora.

Lobelia rhynchopetalum.note: Giant rosette lobelias of the Afroalpine moorland.

Magnoliopsida.note: Flowering plants go from rare to dominant inside forty million years, pulling pollinating insects, fruit-eating birds and the modern structure of forests along with them.

Marchantiophyta.note: Liverwort-grade plants -- the first land vegetation, known from cryptospores rather than bodies.

Mauritia.note: The moriche palm, forming swamp stands across lowland tropical South America; its pollen marks the great Miocene wetland of western Amazonia.

Medullosa.note: Produced the largest pollen grains known.
Medullosa.hb: scrambling or self-supporting, with very large fronds

Medullosales.note: Seed ferns with enormous fronds and the largest seeds of the Palaeozoic.

Metasequoia.note: The dawn redwood, a conifer that drops its needles: it grew inside the Arctic Circle in the Paleocene warmth, and was thought extinct until living trees were found in central China in the 1940s.
Metasequoia.hb: deciduous canopy tree, forming high-latitude forests

Neocalamites.note: A large Triassic and Jurassic horsetail, successor to the Calamites of the Carboniferous swamps.

Noeggerathiopsis.note: A strap-leaved cordaitalean of the Glossopteris flora, growing beside the seed ferns in the cool-temperate forests of Permian Gondwana.

Nothofagus.note: Southern beech forest growing on Antarctica at high southern latitudes -- forest on a continent now under ice.
Nothofagus.hb: canopy tree of cool temperate rainforest

Nymphaeales.note: Water lilies -- one of the earliest-branching flowering plant lineages, and among the first angiosperms in the record.

Nypa.note: A mangrove palm whose pollen turns up in Eocene England and Belgium. For a while the tropics reached far enough north to put mangroves in the North Sea.

Olea laperrinei.note: The Laperrine's olive, a relict of wetter Sahara clinging to the massif's heights.

Picea.note: Spruce, a defining conifer of the boreal forest.

Picea mariana.note: Black spruce, the tree of cold, wet North American muskeg, able to root into sphagnum.

Picea obovata.note: Siberian spruce, the taiga's dominant tree across the range.

Pinus.note: Pine: the most widespread conifer genus, holding poor soils and fire-prone ground since the Cretaceous.

Pinus contorta.note: Lodgepole pine, whose cones open only in fire.

Platanaceae.note: The plane-tree family, among the first flowering plants to become common in Cretaceous floras.

Pleuromeia.note: A metre-tall unbranched lycopod that stands in for an entire vanished forest flora.

Poaceae.note: The grasses. Present from the Late Cretaceous, and ecologically almost invisible until about 40 Ma, when open grassland begins.

Poaceae (C3 grasslands).note: Open grassy country spreads as the world cools and dries after the Eocene, and grazing mammals begin evolving the tall, cement-filled teeth that silica-rich grass demands.

Poaceae (prairie).note: The Great Plains grassland spreads through the Miocene, which is why its horses evolve tall, ever-growing teeth.

Podocarpaceae.note: Southern conifers -- podocarps, rimu, totara -- that clothed warm-temperate Gondwana and still dominate many southern and tropical-mountain forests.

Polylepis.note: Paper-bark trees forming the highest true forests on Earth, above 4,000 m.

Populus euphratica.note: The desert poplar, surviving on groundwater along dry river courses.

Progymnospermopsida.note: Wood-producing plants that still reproduce by spores -- the structural revolution before the reproductive one.

Psaronius.note: A tree fern whose trunk was a mantle of adventitious roots rather than wood. It took over the mires as the giant lycopsids faltered.
Psaronius.hb: tree fern with a mantle of adventitious roots

Ptilophyllum.note: A bennettitalean with stiff fern-like fronds, common through Jurassic and Cretaceous floras.

Quercus.note: Oaks. With beech, the backbone of northern-hemisphere temperate forest, from Mexico's cloud forests to the Himalaya.

Rapateaceae.note: An ancient plant family largely confined to the shield, radiating on the tepui summits.

Raphia.note: Swamp palms bearing the longest leaves of any plant, along the flooded interior.

Rhizophora.note: Mangrove is the one forest that shows up as coastline rather than as interior vegetation, and it is a Cenozoic feature.
Rhizophora.hb: intertidal tree on stilt roots, salt-excluding

Rhododendron.note: Rhododendrons: evergreen shrubs and small trees that band wet mountain slopes by altitude, with their greatest diversity in the Sino-Himalaya.

Rhynia.note: A leafless, rootless Rhynie chert plant preserved cell by cell, and the closest thing we have to a photograph of the first land ecosystem.

Rufloria.note: The characteristic Angaran leaf - cool temperate, seasonal, deciduous.
Rufloria.hb: deciduous tree with strong growth rings

Salix arctica.note: Arctic willow, a centuries-old tree growing flat against the ground.

Sequoia sempervirens.note: The coast redwood, the tallest tree on Earth, in the fog belt.

Sequoiadendron.note: The giant sequoia, largest tree on Earth by volume and a relict of a family once spread across the northern continents.

Sigillaria.note: Tall, usually unbranched, in coal swamps
Sigillaria.hb: tall, usually unbranched, in coal swamps

Stipa.note: Feather grasses whose awns drill their own seed into the soil.

Tamarix.note: Salt-excreting shrubs holding the fringes of oases and wadis.

Umkomasia.note: The seed-bearing organ of Dicroidium, the seed fern that dominated Triassic Gondwana.

Vachellia.note: The flat-topped thorn trees of African savanna, whose spread tracks the Miocene expansion of grassland.

Vertebraria.note: The segmented root of the Glossopteris trees, preserved in Antarctic peat and Indian coal: the plumbing of a forest that grew in polar light.
Vertebraria.hb: septate, air-filled roots in waterlogged soil

Vojnovskya.note: A gymnosperm of the Angaran flora, from a Permian Siberia too cold for the coal swamps of the tropics.

Voltzia.note: A conifer of Triassic river plains, part of the flora that recolonised the land after the end-Permian coal gap.

Voltziales.note: Conifers spreading through the dry Triassic interior: the first forests built by plants that could survive a real dry season.

Walchia.note: An early conifer in drier upland settings -- the beginning of forest that is not a swamp.

Wattieza.note: The Gilboa tree: a trunk topped by a frond crown, and the oldest known forest stand.

Weichselia.note: A fire- and drought-tolerant fern that carpeted Cretaceous floodplains and coastal flats, often the commonest plant fossil beside the dinosaurs.

Welwitschia mirabilis.note: A two-leaved gymnosperm that lives a thousand years on fog alone.

Williamsonia.note: Bennettitales look like cycads and are not; their bisexual cones long confused the search for the origin of flowers.
Williamsonia.hb: stout trunk with a crown of pinnate leaves and flower-like cones

Zosterophyllopsida.note: Sprawling, rhizomatous vascular plants that built the first vegetation dense enough to change how rivers behave.

Zosterophyllum.note: An early vascular plant carrying sporangia along the sides of its stems, on the line that leads to the lycophytes.

angiosperm canopy trees.note: Flowering trees closing a canopy overhead. That structure is what makes a rainforest a rainforest, and it does not exist before the Late Cretaceous.

dwarf birch.note: A low, ground-hugging birch of tundra and the ragged edge of the boreal forest.

epiphytes.note: Plants growing on other plants: orchids, bromeliads, ferns. They need a canopy to live in, so they date it.

lianas.note: Woody climbers using trees as scaffolding to reach the light. Like epiphytes, they exist only where there is a canopy.

seagrass meadows.note: Flowering plants that returned to the sea in the Cretaceous, binding shallow sediment and nursing juvenile fish and turtles.

sedges.note: Cyperaceae: grass-like plants of wet ground, marsh and tundra, where true grasses do less well.

succulents.note: Water-storing plants of arid ground -- cacti in the Americas, euphorbias and aloes in Africa and Arabia, two unrelated answers to the same problem. They spread as the deserts did, from about 30 Ma.
